blocks.heading: Fifty-one percent
text: The phrase gets used as though it meant the end of everything.
It buys a specific and surprisingly short list of powers, and the list of what it does not buy is more interesting.

blocks.heading: One power, several uses
text: A majority of the hashrate means your chain grows fastest. That is the whole capability.
Everything else follows from it, because the network's rule is to follow the chain with the most work.

blocks.alt: Two columns listing what a hashrate majority can do - choose the chain, exclude transactions, reverse recent blocks, take rewards - against what it cannot
blocks.caption: The left column is bad. The right column is the reason the system is still standing.

blocks.heading: How it turns into money
text: Deposit coins at an exchange. Wait out its confirmation policy. Trade for something else and withdraw that.
Then publish the private chain in which the deposit never happened. The exchange is holding nothing; you kept the withdrawal.
Notice what was attacked. Not a signature, not a hash, not the chain's mathematics.
The target was somebody else's decision about how many confirmations were enough - which is exactly the decision Nora had to make in the last lesson.

blocks.heading: What it still cannot do
text: It cannot move coins out of an address. Hashing is not signing, and no quantity of it produces a signature for a key you do not have.
It cannot mint. A block paying itself an over-large subsidy is rejected by every full node, no matter how much work is behind it.

blocks.question: If a majority can rewrite history, why not go back to 2015 and take everything?
answer: Because rewriting from depth $d$ means redoing $d$ blocks of work while the honest chain keeps extending. With 51% you outpace it by a hair, so catching up on a decade takes roughly a decade.
Depth is the defence, and it is the only one that gets stronger by itself while you do nothing.

blocks.heading: Which is fine, until you do not own the hardware
text: A chain's security is paid for by its block reward. So a small chain has a small security budget - and that would be its own business, except for one thing.
If it uses the same proof-of-work algorithm as a much larger chain, the hashrate to attack it can simply be rented by the hour.

blocks.heading: Ethereum Classic, twice
text: Deep reorganisations and double spends against exchanges. The January incident cost in the region of a million dollars; the August attacks reorganised **thousands of blocks**.
Nothing about Ethereum Classic's cryptography failed. It ran an algorithm whose hardware was pointed at a bigger chain, and could be turned around for an afternoon.
Bitcoin Gold, May 2018: double spends against exchanges in the region of 18 million dollars, and attacked again in 2020. Same shape.
The lesson generalises: a chain is not secured by its own hashrate. It is secured by how expensive it is for someone to briefly acquire more.
There is no 51% threshold in any protocol rule. Nothing detects it, nothing triggers, no alarm goes off.
Below a majority the attacks in this lesson still work - just less often, exactly as the curve in lesson 16 says. 51% is where success becomes certain given enough patience, not where it starts.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: Proof of work does not make attacks impossible; it prices them, and the price is set by what the hardware costs to rent, not by what the chain is worth.
One large network looked at that bill and stopped paying it. Next: what it bought instead.
